title: Patterns in Life: Diversity and Classification

topics.title: Why and how we classify living things

learn.hook: India is home to tigers, peacocks, neem trees, tiny bacteria in curd and thousands of kinds of insects. How can anyone study so many living things? By sorting them into groups!
points: Classification is grouping organisms by their similarities and differences. It makes the huge variety of life easier to study and shows how organisms are related.

Important features used for classifying: is the cell prokaryotic or eukaryotic? Is the organism unicellular or multicellular? Does it make its own food (autotroph) or depend on others (heterotroph)? Does it have a cell wall?
Organisms are arranged in a hierarchy of levels: Kingdom → Phylum (Division for plants) → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species.
As we go down from kingdom to species, groups get smaller and members share more and more features.
A species is a group of similar organisms that can interbreed and produce fertile offspring. It is the basic unit of classification.

example.q: Think it through: A neem tree and a mushroom both grow out of the ground and do not move. Why are they placed in different kingdoms?
steps: Look at the mode of nutrition.
The neem tree has chlorophyll and makes its own food by photosynthesis: it is an autotroph.
The mushroom has no chlorophyll and absorbs food from dead and decaying matter: it is a heterotroph.
Their cell walls also differ: cellulose in neem, chitin in mushroom. So neem is in Plantae and mushroom is in Fungi.
example.answer: They differ in nutrition (autotroph vs heterotroph) and cell-wall material, so neem is a plant and mushroom is a fungus.

learn.reallife: The Botanical Survey of India and the Zoological Survey of India identify and classify the plants and animals of our country.

games.prompt: Arrange the levels below Kingdom from the broadest to the narrowest

games.title: Makes its own food or not?

quiz.q: Why do scientists classify living organisms?
options: To make the huge variety of life easier to study and to show relationships
To decide which organisms are useless
To give every organism the same name
To reduce the number of organisms
quiz.explain: Grouping organisms by similarities makes them easier to study and reveals how they are related.
quiz.mistake: Thinks classification judges the value of organisms

quiz.q: Which is the correct order of levels, from broadest to narrowest?
options: Species → Genus → Family → Order → Class → Phylum → Kingdom
Phylum → Kingdom → Class → Order → Genus → Family → Species
Kingdom → Class → Phylum → Family → Order → Species → Genus
Kingdom → Phylum → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species
quiz.explain: The hierarchy starts with the broadest group, Kingdom, and ends with the narrowest, Species.
quiz.mistake: Reverses the order or swaps neighbouring levels

quiz.q: What is the basic unit of classification?
quiz.explain: The species is the smallest, most basic group: similar organisms that can interbreed and produce fertile offspring.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the biggest group is the basic unit

quiz.q: Which level contains the largest number of different kinds of organisms?
quiz.explain: Kingdom is the broadest level, so it includes the most kinds of organisms, which share only a few basic features.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the broadest level with the narrowest

quiz.q: The tiger and the lion belong to the same genus, Panthera. What does this tell us?
options: They are closely related and share many features
quiz.explain: Members of the same genus share many features and are closely related, but they are different species.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the same genus means the same species

quiz.q: Which basic feature separates bacteria from plants, animals and fungi?
options: Bacteria are prokaryotic, with no nuclear membrane
quiz.explain: Bacteria have prokaryotic cells without a membrane-bound nucleus, while plants, animals and fungi are eukaryotic.
quiz.mistake: Picks a feature that bacteria share with plants or fungi, such as a cell wall

quiz.q: A neem tree makes its own food, while a mushroom absorbs food from dead matter. Which feature of classification differs here?
quiz.explain: Making food (autotroph) versus taking food from outside (heterotroph) is a key feature used in classification.
quiz.mistake: Uses unimportant features like colour or size for classification

quiz.q: Which statement best defines a species?
options: Organisms that live in the same place
Similar organisms that can interbreed and produce fertile offspring
All organisms in the same kingdom
quiz.explain: Members of a species can breed with each other to produce offspring that can themselves reproduce.
quiz.mistake: Thinks organisms living together must be one species

teach.ask: Gappu tries to sort the animals in a zoo: "Should I group them by colour? By size? How do scientists decide?"
teach.praise: Chirp! Scientists group living things by important features like cell type, body organisation and mode of nutrition, and arrange them from kingdom down to species!
teach.nudge: Colour can change, but what deeper features, like cells or food, could you use instead?

learn.hook: A mango is 'aam' in Hindi, 'maavu' in Kannada and 'amba' in Marathi. But scientists everywhere call it Mangifera indica. One name for the whole world!
points: Carl Linnaeus, a Swedish scientist of the 18th century, introduced binomial nomenclature, a two-part scientific name for every species.
The first part is the genus name and the second part is the species name, for example Homo sapiens (humans) and Panthera tigris (tiger).
Rules: the genus name begins with a capital letter and the species name with a small letter. In print the name is in italics; when handwritten, the two words are underlined separately.
Scientific names avoid confusion, because local names differ from place to place and language to language.
Indian examples: Azadirachta indica (neem), Mangifera indica (mango), Pavo cristatus (Indian peafowl), Panthera leo (lion), Ficus benghalensis (banyan).

example.q: Think it through: A student writes the scientific name of the tiger as 'panthera Tigris'. What is wrong, and what is the correct form?
steps: The first word is the genus, which must start with a capital letter: Panthera.
The second word is the species, which must start with a small letter: tigris.
In print the whole name is in italics; when handwritten, each word is underlined separately.
example.answer: The capitals are swapped; it should be Panthera tigris.

learn.reallife: Forest officers, doctors and scientists from different countries use scientific names so that everyone knows exactly which plant or animal is meant.

games.title: Match the common name to the scientific name

items.text: Binomial nomenclature was introduced by Carl ___.
In Panthera leo, the word Panthera is the ___ name.
The genus name always begins with a ___ letter.
In print, scientific names are written in ___.

quiz.q: Who introduced the system of binomial nomenclature?
quiz.explain: Carl Linnaeus gave every species a two-part scientific name in the 18th century.
quiz.mistake: Confuses Linnaeus with Whittaker, who proposed the five kingdoms

quiz.q: In the scientific name Mangifera indica, what does 'Mangifera' stand for?
quiz.explain: The first word of a binomial name is always the genus; the second is the species.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the first word is the species

quiz.q: In the scientific name of humans, Homo sapiens, which word must begin with a capital letter?
quiz.explain: The genus name starts with a capital letter and the species name with a small letter, so it is written Homo sapiens.
quiz.mistake: Capitalises both words, as in an ordinary title

quiz.q: What is the scientific name of the tiger, India's national animal?
quiz.explain: The tiger is Panthera tigris. Panthera leo is the lion, Felis catus is the house cat and Pavo cristatus is the Indian peafowl.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the species names within the genus Panthera

quiz.q: Why do scientists use scientific names instead of local names?
options: One scientific name is understood everywhere, while local names differ between places and languages
Scientific names are easier to pronounce
Local names are not allowed in India
quiz.explain: A plant may have many local names, but only one scientific name, so scientists everywhere know exactly which species is meant.
quiz.mistake: Thinks scientific names are used only because they sound important

quiz.q: The lion is Panthera leo and the tiger is Panthera tigris. Which statement is correct?
options: They belong to the same genus but are different species
They belong to the same species
quiz.explain: Both share the genus Panthera, but the different second words show they are different species.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a shared first word means the same species

quiz.q: What is the scientific name of neem?
quiz.explain: Neem is Azadirachta indica. Mangifera indica is mango, Ficus benghalensis is banyan and Oryza sativa is rice.
quiz.mistake: Picks another name ending in 'indica'

quiz.q: How should a scientific name be shown when it is handwritten?
options: With the genus and species words underlined separately
With no capital letters at all
quiz.explain: Handwriting cannot show italics, so each word of the name is underlined separately.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the rule for handwritten scientific names

teach.ask: Gappu's friend from Kerala calls a mango 'maanga' and his friend from Delhi says 'aam': "Which name is right? How do scientists avoid this muddle?"
teach.praise: Tweet! Both local names are fine, but scientists use one binomial name, genus plus species, like Mangifera indica, which is the same all over the world!
teach.nudge: What are the two parts of a scientific name, and why is it better than a local name?

learn.hook: A bacterium in curd, an Amoeba in a pond, a mushroom after the monsoon rain, a lotus and a tiger: one representative from each of the five kingdoms!
points: In 1969 Robert Whittaker proposed the five-kingdom classification: Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia. It is based on cell type, body organisation and mode of nutrition.
Monera: prokaryotic and unicellular. Some make their own food, others do not. Examples: bacteria and cyanobacteria (blue-green algae).
Protista: unicellular eukaryotes. Examples: Amoeba, Paramecium, Euglena and diatoms.
Fungi: eukaryotic heterotrophs, mostly saprophytes that absorb food from dead and decaying matter. Their cell walls contain chitin. Examples: yeast, mushrooms, bread mould (Rhizopus) and Penicillium.
Plantae: multicellular eukaryotes with cellulose cell walls and chlorophyll; they are autotrophs. Animalia: multicellular eukaryotes with no cell wall; they are heterotrophs.

example.q: Think it through: A newly found organism is many-celled, has eukaryotic cells with no cell wall and eats other organisms. Which kingdom does it belong to?
steps: No cell wall rules out Fungi and Plantae, which have cell walls.

learn.reallife: Penicillium, a fungus, gave us the antibiotic penicillin, and cyanobacteria help fix nitrogen in paddy fields, which supports rice crops.

games.title: Match the organism to its kingdom
Five kingdoms: true or false?
items: Bacteria and cyanobacteria have no membrane-bound nucleus.
Fungi make their own food by photosynthesis
Fungi have no chlorophyll; they are heterotrophs that absorb food.
Animal cells do not have a cell wall
Animal cells are bounded only by a cell membrane.
Amoeba belongs to the kingdom Monera
Amoeba is a unicellular eukaryote, so it belongs to Protista.
Chitin is the tough material in fungal cell walls, unlike the cellulose of plants.

quiz.q: Who proposed the five-kingdom classification?
quiz.explain: Robert Whittaker proposed the five kingdoms in 1969.
quiz.mistake: Thinks Linnaeus, who gave binomial names, also gave the five kingdoms

quiz.q: To which kingdom do bacteria belong?
quiz.explain: Bacteria are prokaryotic and unicellular, which places them in Monera.
quiz.mistake: Puts all unicellular organisms in Protista

quiz.q: Amoeba and Paramecium belong to which kingdom?
quiz.explain: They are single-celled eukaryotes, which places them in Protista.
quiz.mistake: Puts them in Animalia because they move and eat

quiz.q: Mushrooms belong to the kingdom Fungi. Which feature do fungi have?
quiz.explain: Fungi are eukaryotic heterotrophs with cell walls made of chitin.
quiz.mistake: Thinks fungi are plants because they do not move

quiz.q: Cyanobacteria (blue-green algae) belong to which kingdom?
quiz.explain: Despite the name 'algae', cyanobacteria are prokaryotic bacteria, so they belong to Monera.
quiz.mistake: Is misled by the word 'algae' in the name

quiz.q: Which kingdom has multicellular eukaryotes with no cell wall that depend on other organisms for food?
quiz.explain: Animals are multicellular heterotrophs whose cells have no cell wall.
quiz.mistake: Picks Fungi, which are heterotrophs but have cell walls

quiz.q: Which description fits the kingdom Plantae?
options: They are multicellular autotrophs with cell walls
quiz.explain: Plants are multicellular eukaryotes with cellulose cell walls and chlorophyll for making their own food.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the features of plants and animals

quiz.q: How do most fungi get their food?
options: By absorbing it from dead and decaying matter
quiz.explain: Most fungi are saprophytes: they release enzymes onto dead matter and absorb the digested food.
quiz.mistake: Thinks fungi make food like green plants

teach.ask: Gappu finds a mushroom under a tree: "It grows in the soil and does not move, so it must be a plant, right?"
teach.praise: Chirp chirp! A mushroom is a fungus, not a plant: it has no chlorophyll, absorbs food from dead matter and has chitin in its cell walls. Fungi are a whole kingdom of their own!
teach.nudge: Does a mushroom have green chlorophyll to make its own food? Where does it get food from?
